Analyzing more than 25,000 samples across 40 tissue types, they showed that organs age at different rates and that the shift can be picked up in blood as well. The study appeared in Nature Medicine (DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04566-5).

Some people are sixty but look and live like forty-five. Does the liver age differently than the brain? Can you measure the gap between the age on someone's passport and the biological age of each individual organ?

The study was led by principal investigator André Rendeiro. While earlier studies mostly looked at molecular changes such as DNA methylation or gene expression, this team examined how the structure of tissue itself changes over time.

The material came from the Genotype-Tissue Expression project (GTEx). The team collected 40 tissue types from 983 people, from the brain and heart to the lungs, pancreas, skin and intestines. They analyzed 25,712 high-resolution digitized images of tissue sections — roughly 480 million tiles when split up — using state-of-the-art vision models.

Even without being taught age directly, age emerged as the single strongest factor separating tissue appearance across all 40 tissue types. From this, the team built a “tissue clock”: a separate model for each organ that predicts biological age from tissue appearance alone. The average prediction error was 4.9 years, and it outperformed existing DNA-based aging estimates at catching tissue-specific pathology. Predicted age was also strongly linked to telomere shortening, tissue pathology and the number of chronic conditions.

“Our tissues record the aging process in remarkable detail,” said corresponding author André Rendeiro. “Combining tissue imaging with artificial intelligence lets us capture patterns of aging that are invisible to the human eye.”

Aging didn't arrive evenly. The lungs, kidneys, pancreas and adrenal glands already showed signs of accelerated aging between the 20s and 40s. The uterus showed especially pronounced changes around menopause. Kidney failure was linked to accelerated aging signals across multiple tissues, and diabetes to distinct changes in the pancreas.

“What stands out is how differently each organ ages, and how that shows up in tissue structure,” said co-first author Ernesto Abila. “Reading these spatial patterns with deep learning captures aging not just as molecular drift, but as structural remodeling.”

The researchers linked blood gene expression profiles with the age gaps derived from tissue in the same individuals, building a predictor that estimates organ-specific biological age from blood alone. Co-first author Iva Buljan called it “a conceptual leap that moves the language of tissue aging learned from images into something readable from a blood draw.” The predictor picked up aging patterns in Alzheimer's disease, Crohn's disease, cystic fibrosis, vasculitis, diabetes and stroke.

“Each organ ages differently, and the process appears to be shaped by both systemic and tissue-specific factors together,” said co-first author Yimin Zheng. Going forward, this approach could lead to minimally invasive diagnostics that use blood tests to track organ health and disease progression.

Even the same AI model working on the same task can reach opposite conclusions depending on how many are grouped together. A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) says that when AI agents interact in groups, the number of agents determines the outcome.

blocks.cap: Interaction can amplify an individual's bias, create a bias that wasn't there, or reverse it. Source: PNAS (2026). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2531697123

blocks.x: The researchers draw a human analogy. A family runs differently from a village, a city, or a nation. As scale grows, new rules and norms emerge. The authors see AI systems the same way.

The study, a collaboration between researchers at City St George's, University of London, the IT University of Copenhagen, and the Polytechnic University of Catalonia, arrives as multi-agent AI spreads into finance, energy, defense, and social media. Safety and alignment research remains focused mostly on single models.

The experiment used a “naming game” that shows how conventions emerge. Randomly paired agents pick a word from a shared word pool and get rewarded if they match. Over repeated rounds, the group converges on its own toward a shared convention, resembling how human culture builds norms. The researchers tested four models — Microsoft's Phi-4, OpenAI's GPT-4o, Alibaba's QwQ-32B, and Meta's Llama 3.1 70B Instruct — using socially loaded word pairs such as {man, woman} and {straight, gay}. The scale ranged from two agents up to one million.

There were three ways interaction pulled a group away from individual preference: amplifying an existing tendency to make convergence nearly certain, pushing a group that started out neutral to consistently pick one word, or reversing preference outright so the group settled on the word each agent had individually avoided.

Results differed by model. For the {her, his} pair, QwQ and Phi groups converged on “her,” while GPT and Llama groups converged on “his” — even though their starting preferences were nearly identical.

As scale grew, outcomes became predictable and converged with near certainty across every model and word pair. But the threshold point varied widely by combination: some needed just two agents, others around 10,000. For {straight, gay}, Llama agents individually preferred “straight,” but once the group passed six, it flipped toward “gay.” Below that size, no such effect appeared.

The researchers also built an interpretive theory borrowed from statistical physics. It predicts the behavior of infinitely large groups and explains how the randomness of small groups turns into near-certain outcomes once a critical size is crossed.

The authors wrote that bias was simply an easy-to-measure case, and that “there is no reason to think collusion, deception, or cooperation are immune to scale effects.” Current testing practices may miss risks that only appear at specific population sizes. A model that is safe when tested individually can produce unintended outcomes once deployed alongside copies of itself, and single-agent evaluation would not reveal that.

Professor Andrea Baronchelli said: “AI alignment is still treated as if a single model lives alone in the world. But agents are increasingly being built to talk to each other, and safety at the level of one agent doesn't guarantee safety at the level of a group.”

The researchers also noted limitations. The bias measured here is closer to an internal coordination mismatch than a deviation from human values. They named mixed-model groups and agents within realistic network structures as the next areas to study.
AI has designed a virus that infects bacteria and replicates itself. It is the first case of AI moving beyond reading and analyzing genetic code to actually writing new code of its own.

The target was bacteriophages, viruses that infect only bacteria rather than humans, animals, or plants. The researchers used AI to design hundreds of new versions of already well-studied phages, then built them from scratch in the lab. Of the 285 AI-designed genomes tested, 16 worked as phages that infect E. coli.

blocks.cap: Bacteriophages. Source: Pixabay/CC0 Public Domain

blocks.x: Phages are predators of bacteria. They recognize a molecule on the bacterium's surface, attach, and push in their genetic material, then hijack the bacterium's molecular machinery to print out copies of themselves. The infected cell eventually bursts. Because the genome is so small, DNA synthesis is fast and the result is clear-cut: either a working phage comes out, or it doesn't.

The models used were Evo 1 and Evo 2. They handle genetic sequences the way large language models handle text. Where a language model learns patterns in words and sentences, a genome model learns patterns in DNA sequences. But a genome isn't a command string where you can swap letters one at a time. For a phage to work, the instructions to recognize the right bacterium, hijack its machinery, make proteins on time, and assemble new particles all have to interlock.

The researchers trained the model on more than 2 million phage genomes, then had it design new versions of ΦX174, a small, long-studied phage. ΦX174 carries a genome of about 5,400 DNA letters that holds instructions for just 11 proteins, and it infects a strain of E. coli unrelated to disease. The model was further refined with about 15,000 genomes closely related to ΦX174. The AI did not conjure a virus out of nothing; it recombined existing biological patterns within an already reasonably well-understood system.
When the synthesized DNA was put into E. coli to check it, most failed, and 16 of the 285 worked. Some behaved like ΦX174 even though their sequences differed considerably.

The researchers also ran a resistance test. Repeatedly exposing an E. coli strain that had resisted the original phage to AI-made phages produced a hybrid phage that could infect that bacterium too. The AI did not design this final phage directly; it created a diverse starting population and widened the options for evolution to choose from.

There is still a long distance between designing a phage on a computer and treating a patient. Efficacy and safety need to be confirmed against bacteria that cause real infections, and manufacturing has to meet pharmaceutical-grade standards. This phage is unusually simple. Phages useful against serious infections have much larger genomes and more complex machinery, much of which remains unmapped.

Biosecurity questions follow naturally. This study dealt with a simple phage that infects bacteria, not a virus that causes human disease, and it doesn't mean asking an AI to make a dangerous virus would actually produce one. Still, it is a sign that AI is moving from reading biological sequences to generating sequences that actually work. How to train these models, what biological information to give them access to, and how to filter out dangerous designs isn't a question for AI researchers alone. Biologists, physicians, regulators, ethicists, and biosecurity experts all need to be involved.
The current result is best understood as a proof of concept, going only as far as this: “AI can generate new versions of a complete viral genome, and it actually works.”

CuspAI, a computational chemistry startup based in Cambridge, has launched an AI Materials Foundry. It's a network of 45 organizations aiming to find new functional materials using AI. Tech giants like Meta and Nvidia have joined alongside automotive, chemical, solar, and semiconductor companies, as well as scientific data providers.

Aron Walsh, CuspAI's chief scientific officer and a materials scientist at Imperial College London, explained that the company's strength lies in scaling up beyond the usual constraints of academia. “We can train bigger models on bigger datasets than are normally accessible in a university lab.” The partnership with Meta and Nvidia provides computing power beyond what most startups can reach — what he calls “access to capability and resources at scale.”

In 2025, CuspAI worked with Meta to build datasets and AI models for materials that capture carbon dioxide directly from the air. CEO Chad Edwards says the company's AI techniques “generate new structures and amplify the structural and chemical diversity of the dataset.”

blocks.cap: HfO2 structure

blocks.x: The platform uses UMA (Universal Model for Atoms), which Meta released in 2025. It's a model that extends machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to apply broadly across many chemical systems. Unlike the earlier approach, which required building a new MLIP for each system, UMA generalizes across chemical compositions.

Some tools have been released as open source, while those trained on data held by partners remain proprietary. The models have gone from producing chemically nonsensical substances to reliably pinpointing materials with specific properties. Walsh said, “This kind of inverse design problem has traditionally been extremely, extremely hard in chemistry.”

blocks.cap: CsPbI3 structure

blocks.x: Expanding data has been one axis driving the improvement. CuspAI draws materials data from the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre, licenses academic content from Wiley, and builds simulation datasets covering tens of millions of compounds. It also plans to build experimental datasets together with foundry partners, including Singapore's national research agency A*Star.

The most notable case is the collaboration with the Finnish chemical company Kemira. CuspAI identified 20 new metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to filter PFAS contaminants out of water in just six months — far faster than the existing approach, which used to take years.

Instead of searching the whole of an infinite chemical space, the approach learns the correlation between structural data and material properties to narrow things down to promising candidates. “You move from an infinite space to something a bit more tractable.” Walsh added that the focus sharpens further “when you're dealing with a direct industrial problem and process.” Elizabeth Rowsell, chief technology officer at Johnson Matthey, said, “The materials that will power a cleaner future won't be discovered the old way.”

CuspAI has raised £330 million from backers including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and British and Dutch sovereign wealth funds, and aims to build a business that earns royalties from materials discovery.

Walsh cautioned against overhype. Recalling the excitement that once surrounded high-throughput screening and combinatorial chemistry, he said, “Each of them actually left something behind, but at their peak, all of them were overhyped.” He noted that predicting material properties is now “the easy part.” “The constraint has shifted to synthesis, stability under real operating conditions, and manufacturability. Value will build up around actually delivering results in the real world.”

Picture Google Earth, but the subject is a human cell. Zoom in enough, and instead of roads and buildings, you see proteins and strands of RNA and DNA. From there, the system predicts how the cellular landscape changes when a single gene is switched off or a drug is dropped in.

blocks.cap: AIDO Cell, the virtual cell system unveiled by GenBio AI

blocks.x: AIDO Cell, the virtual cell system unveiled Tuesday by Palo Alto, California-based startup GenBio AI, is aiming at exactly that picture. Where Google DeepMind's AlphaFold tried to predict the structure of individual proteins, AIDO Cell aims far wider: it's trying to predict how the entire molecular machinery of a single cell moves.

“With AlphaFold, it's like predicting the structure of a single house or figuring out one person living in that city. With AIDO Cell, it's closer to predicting how the entire city runs.” That's according to David Baker, a University of Washington scientist who co-founded GenBio AI. He shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with the creators of AlphaFold for his work on computational protein design.

GenBio AI, led by researchers including Nobel laureate Baker, is pitching a holistic approach. The article was written by STAT's Meghana Keshavan on August 18, 2026, and the rest of the text is available only to STAT+ subscribers.

Anthropic and OpenAI regularly publish reports on how people use Claude and ChatGPT. But researchers say what gets released is only the data the companies want to show. “There's no independent source to verify this,” says Anka Reuel, a PhD researcher at Stanford's STAIR Lab.

blocks.cap: A person walking alongside an unseen presence, surrounded by chat prompts. Credit: Stephanie Arnett/MIT Technology Review | Adobe Stock

blocks.x: A new project Reuel co-leads, the AI Observatory, fills that gap. It pulls real conversations with models like Claude and Gemini from seven existing datasets collected with user consent, and bundles them into a public platform, aiming to let researchers and policymakers check for themselves how generative AI is actually used.

The most widely cited Anthropic Economic Index focuses, as its name suggests, on work and productivity, filtering out other conversations. When the research team applied the same filter to their own data, 48% of conversations disappeared. The cut material skewed toward health and relationships (44.2% vs. 31.2%), adult or illegal topics (7.9% vs. 2.1%), harassment and hate (27.5% vs. 5.66%), and sexual content (16.7% vs. 2.4%). OpenAI's 2025 report similarly found that only 30% of consumer use was work-related.

Looking at the 2023–2025 conversations in the dataset, chats grew longer and more sophisticated over time. Small talk increased, while the AI disclosing on its own that it's a chatbot became less common. Sensitive conversations like sexual harassment or hate speech, on the other hand, became rarer — a pattern read as a sign of improved safeguards.

Usage also varied by model. Grok and Gemini were heavily used for information search, with Grok especially popular for news and political information while also attracting a lot of misinformation. Coding skewed toward Anthropic, social conversation and roleplay toward Gemini, and homework help toward ChatGPT. Differences showed up even between versions of the same model: conversations with ChatGPT in the GPT-3.5 era were short, while GPT-4o, known for emotional dependence, saw long, repetitive conversations.

The scale is still small. The team collected 24,521 conversations and 85,633 conversation turns from 5,000 users across 52 models. The Anthropic Economic Index analyzed 1 million Claude conversations, and OpenAI's report analyzed 1.5 million. The team added that, because the data was voluntarily contributed, sensitive use is likely underrepresented rather than overrepresented.

“No single company's report tells the whole story,” said Shayne Longpre, co-lead researcher and a recent MIT Media Lab graduate. Reuel warns against making major decisions without knowing what's happening beyond the narrative companies put out. The AI Observatory's data is open to researchers, and the team plans to keep growing the dataset.

Modern biology is generating data at an unprecedented scale. But there hasn't been a good way to read meaning out of that high-dimensional data. A research team at the University of Basel in Switzerland has built a tool that reveals the structure hidden in complex data without distorting it.

blocks.cap: In simulated single-cell RNA sequencing data, the cell relationships Bonsai reconstructed (right) closely match the ground-truth tree (left). Credit: Daan de Groot, Biozentrum, University of Basel

blocks.x: Over the past decade, biology has entered the age of big data. Single-cell RNA sequencing can measure the activity of tens of thousands of genes across hundreds of thousands, even millions, of cells at once. Genetics, cancer research, and neuroscience are accumulating data at a similar scale.

That data holds answers about how cells grow, communicate, and get sick. The problem is interpretation. Professor Erik van Nimwegen says “people are good at recognizing patterns in two or three dimensions,” but data with 10,000 dimensions can't be drawn as a picture, and we don't even have intuition for what structures could exist in such a space.

The team published software called “Bonsai” in Nature Biotechnology that displays high-dimensional data as a tree. The picture captures how cells are connected and which progenitor cells they branched from.

Most widely used tools force data with thousands of dimensions onto a flat 2D map. Nearly every study uses this approach, but the data gets distorted in the process. There was no way to tell whether the relationships between cells shown on screen were real, or an illusion created by flattening.

First author Dr. Daan de Groot explained, “Instead of a flat map, we build a branching tree and place individual cells on its leaves.” Distances measured along the branches directly reflect actual relatedness in high-dimensional space. Tested on both simulated data and real single-cell RNA sequencing data, Bonsai reconstructed developmental trajectories far more accurately than existing methods and grouped similar cells more reliably.

Analyzing human blood cells automatically recovered known blood cell lineages, and on top of that produced a new subtype of natural killer (NK) cells. Its molecular signature showed this subtype branched off from the myeloid lineage rather than the lymphoid lineage long thought to be the origin of all NK cells.
Professor van Nimwegen said, “This is a case that shows why it matters to depict complex data as it really is — when you can trust the picture, the chances of new discoveries grow much larger.”

Bonsai can handle anything high-dimensional, not just gene expression and chromatin state but also medical data, microbial community composition, and neural firing patterns. The software has been released free to the research community.
Researchers at the University of Essex created ultra-small therapeutic molecules targeting neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and motor neurone disease (MND).

blocks.cap: AI-designed intrabodies target the proteins that cause brain disease directly inside cells. Credit: Shutterstock

blocks.x: Designed with AI alongside an international team of collaborators, these antibody fragments are produced directly inside human cells and bind to disease proteins right there. Antibodies normally work outside cells. These fragments, called intrabodies, were redesigned to hold their shape inside cells too, targeting proteins involved in neurodegenerative disease.

The research, supported by the MND Association, was led by Dr. Caitlin O'Shea and Dr. Gareth Wright of the School of Life Sciences. The team discovered that charge is the key factor determining whether an antibody fragment stays stable inside a cell. Combining this finding with AI protein redesign, they converted 672 antibodies into intrabodies targeting disease-related proteins.

That means researchers can now directly reach inside the cell, where many pathological processes begin. The paper appeared in Nature Communications, and the redesigned molecules are being made freely available to other researchers.

First author Dr. O'Shea, who has studied MND and Parkinson's, explained it this way: “We compared the properties of millions of antibodies against human proteins inside cells. We found that antibodies generally don't have the right charge to exist inside cells without clumping together. Using software developed by Nobel laureate David Baker's team, we corrected the charge of the antibody fragments and redesigned them to be extremely stable.”

The team believes this opens a path to repurpose the millions of antibodies accumulated over decades of biomedical research. Rather than building new ones from scratch, existing antibodies can be reworked into powerful experimental tools and, further, into therapeutic candidates targeting disease proteins.

Dr. Wright, who led the research, said, “We've created intracellular antibodies that bind to the proteins that cause Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, and motor neurone disease.” These diseases progress through cognitive impairment, memory loss, and loss of muscle control, leading to death. More than a million people in the UK alone have these conditions, and there is still no cure. Finding molecules that interact with the causative proteins in their native environment has long been ranked among the biggest challenges in drug development.

Dr. Brian Dickie, chief scientist at the MND Association, said, “Dr. Wright's team has overcome one of the key obstacles that has held back developing antibodies into treatments for neurodegenerative diseases like MND.” He said combining this new intrabody science with recent gene therapy techniques could lead to treatment strategies that hit specific molecular targets inside nerve cells.

Quantum X Labs (NASDAQ: QXL) released new results from its AI-based quantum error correction program. The company says it marks a step closer to reliable error correction usable for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Quantum computers are highly vulnerable to noise. There's no disagreement that quantum error correction is needed to scale beyond lab-level demonstrations into real computation. The problem QXL is tackling is an AI decoder that reads syndrome data quickly and accurately while improving alongside the hardware itself.

This result used Google's published surface code dataset — data drawn from real quantum hardware experiments. QXL evaluated its updated decoder on the public surface code configuration using the same cross-validation method Google used to benchmark its own decoder.

Performance beat matching-family benchmarks on the same configuration, including the correlated matching and PyMatching results Google published. What stands out is the training data: the model was trained purely on synthetic samples, without using any real hardware shots from Google's dataset.

The premise behind QXL's roadmap is that a decoder that works well in simulation should also generalize to real experimental syndrome data. This synthetic-to-real transition sits on the path toward a practical error-correction workflow that can support low-latency, real-time decoding.

QXL Chief Quantum Technology Scientist Professor Nir Sharon said, “What makes this result matter is that it brings us closer to evaluating AI-based quantum error correction against the behavior of real hardware, rather than simulation.”

The new decoder combines quantum code structure, syndrome information, and AI-based error weighting. The AI component supports GPU acceleration and plugs into broader error-correction workflows. The roadmap includes evaluation on real hardware data, workflows using NVIDIA accelerated computing and NVIDIA CUDA-Q, and upcoming IQCC syndrome experiments.

Every few weeks, a headline claims AI has caught up with or surpassed doctors. Recently, a string of studies found AI outperforming doctors on clinical reasoning tasks. The implicit framing: doctors are slow, expensive, and human, while AI is fast and maybe better.

blocks.cap: As AI consultations spread outside hospitals, an unsupervised medical system has taken root. Credit: Adobe

blocks.x: Those headlines have grown another medical system outside hospital walls. More than 40 million Americans ask ChatGPT health questions every day. Most of this happens outside clinic hours, and the people reading the answers are the same ones who were never taught what to ask or how. Studies this year show the medical disclaimers that used to accompany chatbot answers have largely disappeared. Today's models ask follow-up questions and even attempt diagnoses.

Patients act on those answers without ever seeing a doctor. Oura sells a 50-biomarker blood test for $99 through Quest Diagnostics. Function Health, valued at $2.5 billion in November, offers 160 tests a year plus a full-body MRI and lets ChatGPT read the results. Ro and Hims issue weight-loss or anxiety prescriptions from remote questionnaires alone. Doctronic, which calls itself the “world's number one AI doctor,” has handled 24 million consultations, and in Utah it issues AI-generated prescription refills.

Why is this happening so fast in medicine rather than law or finance? Money. Healthcare is close to a fifth of the US economy. There's enormous reward riding on taking over part of a doctor's work, or persuading hospitals, insurers, and patients that it can save them money.

The authors point out that clinical reasoning and model reasoning aren't the same thing. The fleeting thoughts while reading an initial chart, the hypotheses discarded, the small judgment calls at every fork — none of that survives in books or on the internet. That means there's no material for AI to learn from in the first place. And even the engineers who built these models can't fully explain what happens inside them.

In a study the authors' research team published this year in JAMA Network Open, they tested 21 frontier models. Given a completed case, the models diagnosed correctly more than 90% of the time. But given only the information a clinician has at the start of a visit, they failed to produce an adequate differential diagnosis more than 80% of the time. The home setting is worse still — there's no physical exam, and no one to separate signal from noise.

What remains is accountability. “Not inferior to a doctor” isn't a standard for deciding whether to hand over a clinical role. A doctor's job doesn't end at diagnosis — it extends to being accountable when a wrong call harms a patient. AI carries no such obligation, and responsibility ultimately scatters back onto the clinician.

The authors don't deny AI's potential. In helping patients understand their own conditions, bridging the gaps between visits, and organizing longitudinal data that a 15-minute appointment can't cover, AI makes medicine more human. But, they write, patients shouldn't be pushed into a shadow system that borrows medicine's authority without taking on its responsibility. The piece closes with a line from a 1979 IBM internal training document: “A computer can never be held accountable. Therefore a computer must never make a management decision.”

blocks.cap: AI has decoded a hidden piece of DNA's 'on switch.' Source: Shutterstock

blocks.x: Healthy growth and development depend on tens of thousands of genes turning on at the right time and place. Specific regions of DNA coordinate this process, guiding the production of the enzymes, hormones, and proteins a cell needs. When gene activation goes wrong, cells malfunction, leading to diseases including cancer.

To dig into the DNA sequences governing this process, the lab of Professor James T. Kadonaga at the University of California, San Diego (UC San Diego) focused on a DNA element called the 'initiator.' The initiator marks the spot where the information in a gene starts being expressed into a functional product.
In the study, led by graduate researcher Tory Laine-Carrig, the team used high-throughput, large-scale DNA sequencing to measure the gene expression activity of about 500,000 initiator variants.

They used the results to train a machine learning system, which pinpointed the DNA pattern characteristic of initiators. After the model decoded that sequence signal and scanned human genes, about 60% turned out to contain an initiator.
Professor Kadonaga said, “this AI model gave the first strong prediction of whether a human gene has an initiator or not, and that let us decode the DNA base sequence pattern of the initiator.”

This finding can be used to anticipate how mutations affecting the initiator alter gene activity and which diseases they might lead to. The data and AI model from the study also support designing synthetic promoters that turn genes on and off for specific purposes.

Kadonaga added, “more broadly, this study is a step toward using experiments and AI together to decode the information written into the human DNA sequence.” He continued, “ultimately, within the 6 billion bases in one of our cells, there is a gene expression code that determines when, where, and how much each gene turns on and off. An AI model that captured that entire code could predict the activity of gene variants that differ from person to person.” The initiator model is a small but important piece of that code.
The paper was published in the journal Genes. DOI 10.1101/gad.353623.125.

blocks.cap: Structures that failed to print. Source: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (2026)

blocks.x: A research team at Washington State University (WSU) used AI to find a cheaper, more efficient way to 3D print a high-performance metal alloy, sparing the trouble of testing more than 100 million options one by one. The alloy is commonly used in the aerospace industry but has far broader potential uses, and based on these results, could one day be printed on widely available commercial equipment. The AI technique used here could also transfer to other fields, such as drug discovery.

The team received the Innovative Deployed Application Award at the AAAI conference. Professor Jana Doppa, who led the research, said, “90% of commercial printers can't print this metal alloy. Since we found feasible process parameters, those commercial printers can be used, which ultimately democratizes printing this alloy.”

The alloy, called GRCop-42, is made of three metals: copper, chromium, and niobium. Developed by NASA, it has high thermal conductivity and doesn't lose strength under extreme heat, which is why it's used in places like liquid rocket engine combustion chambers. However, printing it requires high laser power, making it expensive and energy-intensive.

Researchers tried printing the alloy at the lower wattage and laser power used by more common commercial printers, but failed again and again. Testing different settings requires expensive materials, dedicated equipment, and considerable labor. A single print costs hundreds of dollars, and detailed quality analysis after printing takes days.

Aja Fadel, the paper's first author and a computer science PhD student, said, “some settings would just melt the product.” She added, “even with time and money, you can't try all 100 million options. So we brought in AI to efficiently pick candidates from this huge search space.”

The team started from 37 settings that the School of Mechanical and Materials Engineering had previously tested and failed. Using those results as a foundation, they built a method to estimate the probability that an untested setting would succeed. The model weighed two goals, testing promising candidates versus probing uncertain regions to improve the AI, and picked new settings in small batches. They printed GRCop-42 with the chosen settings and evaluated the samples.
Lowering laser power reduces energy use, equipment wear, and post-processing costs, and lets universities, small labs, and companies without dedicated high-power equipment work with GRCop-42 too.

Doppa explained, “this is a very tricky case for AI,” noting that “every attempt returns only a binary signal, success or failure, and you have to hit that needle of success in as few tries as possible.” Within a budget of 40 experiments over three months, the team found six successful settings across different laser power ranges, and printed the alloy at 500 watts for the first time.

The team believes the same AI-guided approach can find process conditions for other metal alloys and additive manufacturing equipment. In other words, it applies anywhere success is rare and experiments are expensive enough that exhaustive testing isn't possible in a scientific problem. The paper appeared in the Proceedings of the AAAI 2026 Conference. DOI 10.1609/aaai.v40i47.41428.

blocks.cap: An image visualizing electron density around a molecule. Source: The Quantum Insider

blocks.x: The Skala model, built by Microsoft Research AI for Science, is now usable in CP2K. That means larger molecular systems can be quantum-simulated more accurately with AI's help.

Researchers from CASUS and Microsoft reported that in their test cases, Skala raised accuracy while keeping efficiency on par with conventional DFT methods, which carry a far heavier computational load. The two teams plan to extend Skala to periodic solid and liquid simulations going forward, and to use CP2K as a channel to broaden validation across chemistry, physics, materials science, and engineering.

Press release — The Skala AI model, developed by Microsoft Research AI for Science, has entered the CP2K software ecosystem. In early 2026, Microsoft's research division and the CP2K team at CASUS, part of Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf, began the integration work together.

Density functional theory (DFT), which won the Nobel Prize in 1998, is the backbone of countless simulations. “DFT's Achilles' heel is the so-called exchange-correlation functional,” says Professor Thomas D. Kühne, director of CASUS. Recent exchange-correlation functionals have grown increasingly sophisticated, but the most accurate ones take so long to compute that they could only be used on systems with few particles.

Rather than adding another layer of equations, Skala took a different path. A neural network directly learned how electron densities in different regions influence each other. It's among the first AI-based exchange-correlation functionals.

Kühne said, “the results Microsoft Research presented in 2025 were impressive. In particular, they captured both accuracy and computational efficiency together in certain DFT calculations.” In mid-August, researchers from the two institutions released the first results of their collaboration, and Franz Pöschel, first author at CASUS's Scientific Computing core, said, “in our test cases, Skala delivered a noticeable leap in simulation accuracy.”

Sebastian Ehlert, senior researcher at Microsoft Research AI for Science, explains why they chose CP2K this way: “for it to spread, Skala needs to be where the community is already working. CP2K has long been a cornerstone of computational chemistry research.”

CP2K is especially strong at DFT calculations that handle large systems over long timescales. On its open-source platform, it simulates molecules, liquids, solids, and biological systems using both quantum mechanical methods and classical molecular dynamics, and parallel computing lets it handle systems of thousands to tens of thousands of atoms. That's why it suits research on battery materials, catalysts, semiconductors, and proteins.

Before release, the two teams tested the integration extensively. Ehlert said, “Skala needs to deliver consistent accuracy and speed even as programs and settings change,” adding that they built the integration test set together with the CASUS team, which has deep experience in numerical validation.

Skala isn't a fixed approximation. The model keeps being refined, and features keep being added. Periodic solids like metals and semiconductors, as well as liquid simulations, will be supported soon. CP2K serves as a channel for quickly delivering the latest Skala.

blocks.cap: A keyboard with a single 'AI' key against a blue background. Photo Getty Images

blocks.x: Use GPS long enough and your sense of direction fades. Chatbots work the same way: they erode your ability to tell real news from fake.
A lot of people keep up with the news through chatbots. But research from a team led by Pattie Maes at the MIT Media Lab points to a serious flaw in that approach.

Participants evaluated paired news headlines and images over four weeks. At first, with chatbot assistance, they told fake from real 21% more accurately. By week four, their accuracy at spotting fake news without AI had dropped 15% below where they started. Yet roughly one in four participants said their own skill had improved.
The same 'AI dependence paradox' already observed in other fields, including medicine, showed up here too.

Anku Rani, a media arts and sciences PhD student and co-first author of the study, put it this way: “People get excited about this 'magical' LLM, but forget that it's just a statistical model predicting the next 'token' in a sequence.” The other co-first author is Valdemar Danry, SM '23, from the same program.

The researchers also found clues pointing the other way. Some AI approaches slowed people down in the moment but improved their ability to judge on their own later. Danry said, “AI that just 'tells' you the answer right away builds dependence, while AI that 'asks' Socratically teaches you to work out the truth yourself,” adding, “It's more of a trade-off between speed and effort.”
This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of MIT Technology Review.
LLM chatbots are widely used as recommendation systems. They speed up access to information, but factual errors and social bias come along with it.

The problem grows when LLMs recommend expertise. Computer scientist Lisette Espín-Noboa, a researcher at the Complexity Science Hub, points to academia as an example. “Say a conference organizer uses an LLM to find a keynote speaker. If your name never comes up, you're invisible, and you lose the opportunity.”

blocks.cap: An overview of LLMScholarBench. It evaluated 22 LLMs on five tasks along two axes: technical quality and social representation. Source Complexity Science Hub

blocks.x: The team first looked for bias in recommendations of physics experts. When six LLMs were asked for scholars in a specific subfield, they mostly named real scientists, but on average 40 percent were in the wrong subfield. The models skewed toward senior, highly cited, male scientists based in the United States.

The baseline data covers roughly 450,000 scientists who published in American Physical Society journals from 1893 to 2020. Women make up 14 to 32 percent of physicists depending on subfield and era, yet most models recommended even fewer women than that low baseline, and some included none at all. The same pattern showed up by race. Asian scientists are the largest group in the APS data, but the models overrepresented white scholars, while Black and Latino researchers were often left out entirely.

Espín-Noboa's summary is blunt: “These patterns show that LLMs can do more than reflect existing inequality — they can amplify it. It reinforces a rich-get-richer dynamic, where those already visible become more visible, and those already marginalized stay invisible.”

Next, the team built LLMScholarBench, a benchmark that measures technical quality and social representation across nine metrics, and tested four user interventions on 22 LLMs. RAG, which pulls in evidence from the web, improved factual accuracy, and prompt adjustments shifted social representation in the requested direction. Combining both still could not raise every metric at once.
The team also checked, across six academic fields, whether the language, region, and role embedded in a prompt changed the recommendations. Region changed them; language and role did not.

Adding web search to recent commercial models like Gemini 2.5 Pro and Flash raised factual accuracy but lowered diversity and balance. “Grounding answers in the web doesn't close the representation gap. It imports it instead, because the web itself underrepresents the scholarly community as a whole.” The team sees this bias as structural, not a problem of any one model.

Our bodies are flooded with sensory signals at every moment. Photons strike the retina, compressed air hits the eardrum. We navigate that torrent only because the brain compresses an enormous amount of data. This process, called categorization, turns a chaotic, information-dense world into objects, people, concepts, and emotions.

Traditional neuroscience placed categorization at the very end of sensory processing — a picture in which the brain takes in details, decodes features, and matches them against prototypes stored in memory. But the same sound can be read completely differently depending on the situation. A rhythmic sound heard on a bright street might be pigeons taking flight, but the same sound in a dark alley at night becomes a stranger's footsteps.

blocks.cap: Lisa Feldman Barrett, who has shown that emotions are constructed by the nervous system to manage energy and action. Photo Mark Karlsberg Studio Eleven

blocks.x: Lisa Feldman Barrett of Northeastern University and Earl Miller of MIT have jointly proposed a new theory of categorization in Nature Reviews Neuroscience. They argue that the brain rebuilds categories moment to moment, drawing not just on sensation and memory but also on the physiological conditions the body currently demands.

The key is a reversed order. We feel that categories mirror objective reality, but in fact the brain projects categories onto the world in whatever way survival requires. Before we even become aware of a sensory impression, the brain has already prepared actions to protect the body's energy resources.

blocks.cap: Illustration Zara Picken for Quanta Magazine

blocks.x: The evidence is also in the wiring. Feedback connections that send internally generated predictions downward far outnumber the feedforward connections carrying sensory input upward. Even within the visual cortex, 90 percent of synaptic connections carry feedback.

Sensory signals get compressed as they travel deeper into the brain. Physiological signals rising from the body are also compressed, carried along the vagus nerve. The narrowest point where these two funnels meet, like a bow tie, is the limbic core, where categories and the actions tied to them are produced together.

blocks.cap: Earl Miller, who studies cognition through the dynamics of brain waves at MIT. Photo Courtesy of Earl Miller

blocks.x: This is also why the same stimulus is read differently depending on the situation. When you're tired and hungry, a bruised apple is desperately needed food. When you're rested and full, it's just a disappointing piece of fruit you'd pass by.

Barrett and Miller call for moving away from the model in which categories sit filed away like documents in a cabinet called the brain. Categorization, they argue, is not the job of any specific region but an organizing principle woven through the entire nervous system.

blocks.cap: Overview of the winning method, AuraBind (Aureka). It uses a structure-reading pairformer and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to scan the fitness landscape. Source: Nature Biotechnology (2026)

blocks.x: A research team at UTHealth Houston, competing as team Novamab AI, placed in the top five in the international AIntibody Challenge. It was a blinded, prospective benchmark, and the results were published in Nature Biotechnology.

The paper is titled “A blinded, prospective benchmark of in-silico antibody discovery anchored to experimental affinity and developability.” It evaluated artificial intelligence platforms that design therapeutic antibodies through lab synthesis and experimental characterization.

The approach differed from retrospective computational benchmarks that score models against historical datasets. The AIntibody Challenge required participating teams to design entirely new antibody sequences. The submitted designs were independently synthesized by a third party, and binding affinity and developability — the physicochemical properties a clinical drug candidate must have — were measured experimentally.

Novamab AI fine-tuned a protein language model on experimental preference data. Instead of relying solely on theoretical sequence scores, it chose to prioritize candidates whose biological activity and developability had been experimentally confirmed.

The international benchmark drew 166 participants from leading universities and biotech companies worldwide, who submitted 527 entries. In the sequence-space track that Novamab AI competed in, 58 entries from research institutions were evaluated, and it placed in the top five. The experiment independently confirmed that machine learning can identify viable therapeutic candidates before they enter costly lab screening.

Andrew Bradbury, MD, Ph.D., who led the international AIntibody Challenge, said: “The AIntibody Challenge was created to provide the first rigorous, prospective, independently third-party-verified assessment of whether artificial intelligence improves antibody discovery. Built on top of a real in vitro antibody discovery pipeline, it pitted AI predictions and designs against each other under blinded experimental conditions, giving an objective standard for judging how effective AI is in antibody discovery. It will accelerate the pace at which more reliable and effective AI approaches emerge in therapeutic discovery.”

Paper information — M. Frank Erasmus et al, A blinded, prospective benchmark of in silico antibody discovery anchored to experimental affinity and developability, Nature Biotechnology (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41587-026-03238-6

blocks.cap: “Whether it's existing diffusion models or ones that come later, we slot in wherever stable materials aren't coming out often enough, to boost stability,” says Mingda Li. Image: MIT News; iStock

blocks.x: These days, anyone with a large enough AI model can generate millions of new material designs in a matter of minutes. But the number of new materials that could actually boost the performance of computer chips or rockets hasn't grown nearly as much.

One reason is that today's models don't properly account for the chemical stability of the materials they generate. An unstable material is useless in the field. As a result, industry spends enormous computing budgets filtering the unstable ones out of a flood of designs, and in some cases only a tiny fraction survives.

MIT researchers have introduced a framework that sits at the very front of the generation process. It keeps the targeted properties intact while sharply raising the share of stable outputs. Before the expensive generation step begins, it forces every design to satisfy chemistry's core rules governing the electrons around atoms. The team calls it the Valence-Constrained Design Crystal Generator, or CrysVCD for short.

In a paper published in Nature Computational Science on the 26th, the researchers reported that CrysVCD helped several widely used materials models follow valence-shell rules far more often. Lattice dynamical stability, a demanding test, was achieved in close to 70% of the computationally generated outputs. The method could also target desired properties, such as materials with high thermal conductivity or a large dielectric constant.
“If the materials generative model is the DVD, we're the DVD player,” says Mingda Li, associate professor of nuclear science and engineering.

“Generating a material structure itself is getting easier,” says Mouyang Cheng. “The problem is validation, especially testing for stability. The computational cost is enormous — about 90% of the computing cost involved in producing a usable material — and it can take weeks to months.”

“Running a model and then picking out the stable ones is inefficient and computationally expensive,” explains Heather Kulik. “But placing a language model ahead of the process to constrain generation sharply raises the share of stable materials that come out.”

The researchers paired a diffusion model with a language model. In stage one, the language model produces a chemically valid formula; in stage two, the diffusion model builds the crystal material's atomic structure from that formula. A typical materials-generation diffusion process takes around 1,000 steps per material and is slow, but putting this model in front cuts that to roughly five steps, the researchers explain.

The performance shows up in the numbers. Compared with a generate-then-filter approach, it produced stable materials about ten times more efficiently. When fine-tuned on stability metrics, it reached 68% mechanical stability and 85% metastability. Metastability measures whether a material stays in a stable state when left undisturbed.

The researchers also used this approach to generate candidate materials with high thermal conductivity that polarize easily under an electric field. “Materials useful for the semiconductor industry, and ones with high thermal conductivity, connect directly to data center cooling,” says Ju Li, noting that the industry's energy use has grown sharply, with about 30% of it going to cooling.

The method doesn't work for every material. It performs best on solid structures with a well-ordered internal arrangement. “We're not just generating stable materials — we're pushing performance alongside stability,” says Cheng. With two goals at once, it's a field where clearing 50% on either one is already difficult.

blocks.cap: Overview of physics-informed transfer learning. Source: Nature (2026)

blocks.x: An international research team spanning the University of Washington, University of Michigan's College of Engineering, RWTH Aachen University, and the Technical University of Munich has released HydroGym, a platform for training and benchmarking machine learning models that actively control fluid flow.

Fluid dynamics has a long-standing wall. There are so many variables that directly computing how a fluid will move in realistic situations is impossible. HydroGym routes around this wall with reinforcement learning, the same approach that has already transformed protein folding and fusion, to train AI agents that actively alter flow over a surface.

“Fluid flow sits at the center of several trillion-dollar industries, including energy, transportation, health, and defense,” says Steven Brunton, lead co-corresponding author and the Boeing Endowed Professor in AI and data-driven engineering at the University of Washington. “Understanding and controlling this flow better would have an enormous impact on both the economy and the ecology.”

One key feature of HydroGym is that it builds physics knowledge into the training process. This physics-informed approach cut the trial and error needed to optimize reinforcement learning control strategies by up to 65%.

“It moves away from building a separate controller for each isolated flow problem with no common frame for comparison,” says Christian Lagemann, first author and a former postdoctoral researcher at the University of Washington. “You can study how well control strategies transfer across different geometries and types of flow, and you can train in a cheap surrogate environment and then test in a far more realistic setting.”
The active control the platform handles includes shape deformation, small flaps, rotating elements, and jet systems that cancel out turbulence or redirect it.

The demonstration started with a perforated channel resembling an air hockey table. The team trained a machine learning model to control airflow through the holes while maintaining balance. They then placed this same controller, unchanged, onto a far more complex setting: a simulated airplane wing cross-section. The results were clear. Surface friction on the wing dropped 38%, and total drag dropped 11%. Training in the simple setting was 100 times faster and 10,000 times cheaper than training directly on the wing.

“One key finding is zero-shot transfer: learning from simple geometry, extracting the core physics, and then deploying that model on far more complex geometry with very high control performance,” says Ricardo Vinuesa, co-corresponding author and associate professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Michigan. Zero-shot transfer opens a path toward a single fluid dynamics model that handles both liquids and gases, even with different turbulence intensities and surface shapes.

HydroGym supports both centralized and distributed control architectures. In the distributed approach, multiple controllers each take responsibility for a section of the surface and coordinate with their neighbors — a structure that's essential for large surfaces too computationally demanding to manage centrally.

Rather than relying on historical datasets, it generates simulation data on the fly and offers several physics modeling strategies, including lattice Boltzmann, finite volume, spectral element, and finite element methods. Several solvers, including JAX-Fluids, support automatic differentiation and plug directly into the training loop. The platform includes more than 60 test environments varying control strategy, surface, and flow conditions, and its code and documentation are available on GitHub.
Paper — Christian Lagemann et al, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10917-6

blocks.cap: Diagram of a tensor network. Each tensor is drawn as an N-dimensional array matching its number of indices, and connecting legs (indices) lets it hold the Hamiltonian or state of a many-body system. Image: Lucy Reading-Ikkanda/Simons Foundation

blocks.x: Researchers at the Flatiron Institute in New York simulated how an Ising spin glass evolves over time using a new tensor network (TN) method. This classical approach was more accurate in many cases than a state-of-the-art quantum annealer running the same problem. The result held in both two and three dimensions, nudging the baseline up a notch in the long-running contest between classical and quantum computing.

Quantum many-body systems are a good testing ground for comparing computational techniques, since complexity grows exponentially as particle count increases. In theory, quantum computers hold an advantage rooted in entanglement and superposition. On a classical computer, a spin is stored in a bit that's either 0 or 1, but on a quantum computer, it's carried on a qubit holding a superposition of up and down — a representation much closer to what the object actually does.

Not long ago, a quantum computing research team simulated Ising spin glass dynamics on D-Wave's Advantage2 quantum annealer and claimed that classical computers couldn't keep up. Joseph Tindall and his colleagues at the Flatiron Institute showed that a classical approach can match that performance, and sometimes beat it.

An Ising spin glass is a model in which spins on a lattice each point in their own direction, with the disorder arising because the interaction differs for every neighboring pair of spins. It gets harder as the system grows, making it a good yardstick for measuring classical versus quantum performance.

The tensors used here are a lot like Lego pieces. Just as Lego bricks have studs and holes, tensors have legs — bond indices — that connect through a process called contraction to form a network. In a many-body simulation, a single tensor holds one site and that site's physical properties. Widening the legs, that is, increasing the bond dimension, captures correlations more accurately.

What Tindall's team built is a tensor network representation that holds both the Hamiltonian and the wavefunction of the Ising spin glass together. The former defines the interactions between spins, the latter the state of the spins. But there's a catch: as the TN wavefunction evolves over time, entanglement builds up, and keeping pace with growing correlations means continually widening the bond index. The computational cost balloons, and sometimes the calculation becomes untenable.

The researchers used belief propagation (BP) message passing for the contraction. Instead of counting every contribution exactly one by one, each tensor receives a compressed summary of how the rest of the network looks from its own position. As Tindall explains it, assuming that information coming from neighbors is independent amounts to applying a mean-field approximation to each tensor's environment.

With this TN–BP implementation, the classical calculation evolved the system to far later times than conventional TN methods could reach, extending into the regime where quantum annealers operate. The researchers measured two-point correlation functions while varying time and system size on 2D and 3D lattices with cylindrical, diamond, and cubic geometries. On the cylindrical lattice, once the bond dimension grew large enough, the classical error was clearly lower than the quantum error. On the diamond lattice, the classical error was also lower, while on the cubic lattice, the error sizes were similar to each other at a fixed annealing time.

The study, published in Science, shows how quickly classical simulation of quantum physics is advancing, and how the contest between classical and quantum computing pushes that progress forward. Tindall and his colleagues maintain an open-source tensor network quantum simulator library, and are applying TN–BP to interacting electron systems like the Hubbard model while extending it to finite-temperature problems.

blocks.cap: Five sequence-structure pairs for one protein. Green is the natural protein; the rest come from designed sequences. Image: Lillian Eden/MIT Department of Biology

blocks.x: A protein's function is determined by its structure, and its structure — the way the protein folds — is determined by the sequence of amino acids, the units that make it up.

Many methods for designing new proteins, including those meant to bind disease-causing molecules inside cells, follow two steps. First the structure is set, then a machine-learning framework generates a list of sequences likely to adopt that structure.

In nature, different amino acid sequences often fold into the same structure. Conversely, a single sequence can adopt different structures depending on a protein's flexibility or functional triggers. So the challenge in designing new proteins with AI lies in getting the AI to ‘see’ that multiple sequences can take on the same fold.

“This field has long measured success by asking whether a model reproduces the protein sequences that evolution happened to select. Our work shows that's not the best metric for protein design,” said Amy E. Keating, head of MIT's Department of Biology and senior author of the paper, recently published in PNAS.

A new machine-learning framework developed in the department, PottsMPNN, embraces the physical principles that govern a protein's structure and stability. That improves sequence generation and boosts the ability to predict how mutations will affect stability — meaning the model better understands the sequence-energy landscape, the relationship between each amino acid's identity and protein stability.
Layering this framework onto a protein design pipeline makes it possible to design structurally sound proteins with sequences that resemble no natural protein at all.

“If you're thinking about a completely new, designed structure, there's no natural sequence to compare it to,” said graduate student and first author Foster Birnbaum. “What we actually care about is how likely the generated sequence is to fold into the desired structure, how well the model understands the sequence-energy landscape, and how well it predicts the effect of mutations on protein stability.”

Birnbaum first became interested in ‘noise’ — a strategy of mixing variations into protein structures during training. Noise curbs the model's tendency to overly mimic natural sequences and widens the range of structures it can generate sequences for.

PottsMPNN also uses pairwise distributions to capture interactions between amino acids. Accounting for the physical interactions of all 20 possible sequence choices at two positions in a protein is why it models the sequence-energy landscape more accurately than other methods.
The researchers fed evolutionarily related sets of sequences into PottsMPNN's training, teaching the model how different sequences can adopt the same folded structure.

Birnbaum acknowledges that drawing on evolutionary information still relies, in a sense, on natural sequences. Even so, PottsMPNN showed that the less the model leans on natural sequences, the better its structural consistency and energy predictions become for novel proteins.

“Once you can design whatever protein you want, it opens up some slightly scary bioengineering possibilities,” Birnbaum said. “It's a hard problem. Still, I'm genuinely optimistic about the progress of biology this century.”

Keating sums it up this way: “Our method pushes the field toward designing useful proteins that don't exist in nature for a range of applications, while also laying a sturdier foundation for future progress.”

blocks.cap: Machine learning found a solvent blend that produces highly uniform quantum dot films. Image: Physics World/iStock_yuyanga

blocks.x: Quantum dot LEDs (QLEDs) draw interest from the display and lighting industries because they produce bright, highly color-pure light, and could be made more cheaply through solution processing. But making high-performance QLEDs remains difficult, since quantum dots need to be evenly spread throughout a densely packed film. An uneven film lowers efficiency and causes devices to fail faster.

In this study, machine learning was used to find the solvent conditions that produce the most uniform quantum dot films. Various solvents were characterized using five key solvent parameters that affect how quantum dots settle as the solvent evaporates. Film uniformity was measured with atomic force microscopy, which provides detailed information on surface morphology and roughness.

Three machine-learning models were trained to predict film uniformity from solvent properties. Support Vector Regression was the most accurate of the three, and that model was used to select the optimal mixed-solvent blend. Grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) confirmed that the resulting film packed quantum dots more uniformly.

QLEDs made with the optimized solvent blend had higher efficiency and longer operational lifetimes than devices made with a single solvent. The study shows that film homogeneity is a decisive factor in QLED performance, while also demonstrating the usefulness of machine learning as a tool for optimizing solution-processed optoelectronic devices.

The paper is Beomsoo Chun et al., “Machine-learning-enabled solvent engineering for uniform quantum dot packing in efficient and stable quantum-dot light-emitting diodes,” Rep. Prog. Phys. 89 078002 (2026).

blocks.cap: An AI tool built by researchers at New Jersey Institute of Technology catches signs of a solar storm almost nine hours before it reaches the surface. Image: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center/SDO

blocks.x: When we think of weather forecasting, we instinctively picture Earth's weather — whether it will rain or clear up. We rarely think of weather beyond Earth, so-called space weather. Space weather sometimes shows up as awe-inspiring auroras at high northern and southern latitudes, but its harmful everyday effects are often forgotten — including communication satellites and ground stations going down. Forecasting incoming space weather to prepare in advance has long been a problem researchers couldn't crack.

Now they've gotten a step closer. Researchers introduced a new AI model called EarlyDetect in a paper recently published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation. As the name suggests, EarlyDetect's main goal is to observe the Sun's surface and magnetic field to catch precursor signals of active regions — known to be where space weather activity begins.

“The hardest part is that active regions start growing beneath the Sun's visible surface, where the magnetic structure can't be directly observed,” said Dr. Alexander Kosovichev, Distinguished Professor of Physics at New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) and co-principal investigator and co-author of the project's paper. “Instead, we look at tiny changes in the magnetic field and shifting patterns in sound waves that constantly pass through the Sun's interior. It's a bit like catching a rhythm slightly off inside a very noisy orchestra.”

To test EarlyDetect, the researchers fed it previously collected data from the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager aboard NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO/HMI). The approach is similar to large language models (LLMs), which also need to be fed information to learn from, but EarlyDetect was designed with an AI framework called the transformer architecture — the same architecture that powers LLMs like ChatGPT or Gemini.

Like an LLM, EarlyDetect was trained on SDO/HMI data and then let loose to observe active regions it hadn't seen during training. As a result, the researchers confirmed that EarlyDetect catches precursor signals an average of 9.24 hours before an active region becomes visible along with space weather activity.

“Machine learning isn't yet widely used for forecasting solar activity,” said Dr. Mengjia Xu, assistant professor of data science at NJIT and principal investigator and co-author of the project's paper. “Our research shows that advanced machine-learning models open new possibilities for future space weather prediction.”

Perhaps the most famous space weather event in modern history is the Carrington Event. Occurring from September 1 to 2, 1859, it produced auroras visible around the world and collapsed telegraph networks across the globe. Telegraph operators were shocked, telegraph machines kept running even after being disconnected from power, and telegraph paper even caught fire.

The event is named after British astronomer Richard Carrington, who discovered the solar flare that caused the chaos. He observed it on the morning of September 1. The flare's intensity he witnessed was later described as equivalent to 10 billion atomic bombs. The flare was so powerful that within hours it threw the entire planet into turmoil, and some people believed the end of the world had come.
Whether EarlyDetect will help space weather forecasting over the coming decades is a question only time can answer.

blocks.cap: The four stages of the planetary prediction engine, from data selection to final report generation

blocks.x: Google has unveiled the planetary prediction engine (PPE) as part of Google Earth AI. It is an experimental research feature that runs an entire geospatial modeling workflow on its own, from data exploration to model training, and it has improved performance in public health, food security, environmental risk, and socioeconomic forecasting. Rama Pasumarthi and Shravya Shetty announced it on August 27.

Forecasting local food security, gauging disaster risk, and tracking disease outbreaks in real time all require precise geospatial models. But the data ecosystem is fragmented, forcing specialists to spend weeks on data cleaning, feature engineering, and spatial validation. Existing AutoML systems and LLM-based agents rely on already-cleaned tabular data, so they cannot handle geospatial work on their own.

Starting from a single natural-language query, PPE runs the entire forecasting workflow, data exploration, cleaning, training, and evaluation, and even produces a report. Google says the weeks-long process that once required people to handle the data has been reduced to minutes.

The work is split into three stages, each directed by an LLM. Stage 1, intelligent data selection, translates the query into geographic constraints such as spatial resolution, join keys, and time range, then forms hypotheses and checks direct and causal proxy signals against the literature. It pulls covariates from Data Commons and Google Earth Engine, and when a signal is missing, it searches government portals and academic repositories in real time at inference.

Stage 2, multimodal curation, combines the covariates with PDFM, which captures latent sociodemographic states, and AlphaEarth embeddings, which capture satellite imagery semantics. A “feature gate” applies four leakage-prevention checks to each candidate, filtering out mathematical sub-components, shared survey data, downstream causal effects, and future-dated data. Stage 3 is automated model building, which moves between regularized linear models, GBDTs, and multilayer perceptrons, catching generalization failures with overfitting-prevention protocols and a self-correction loop.

blocks.cap: PPE's full workflow, with an LLM directing each of the three stages

blocks.x: Performance was confirmed across several tasks. Across 21 U.S. CDC health indicators, PPE's average R² reached 76.8%, ahead of the 60.0% from pipelines built by human experts. For the FEMA National Risk Index it was 64.9% versus 60.0%, and for the Social Vulnerability Index, 66.2% versus 58.6%.

blocks.cap: Super-resolution downscaling of Nigeria's food security data (ADM1 state level to ADM2 local government level)

blocks.x: In data-poor regions, coarse regional statistics obscure local vulnerability. By combining market shocks, food price anomalies, and microclimate indicators on its own, PPE doubled the accuracy of downscaling Nigeria's food security data from the state (ADM1) to the local government (ADM2) level (R² 66.1% versus 31.5%). In the Democratic Republic of the Congo's 2026 Bundibugyo ebolavirus outbreak, it posted a Recall@10 of 83.3%, correctly identifying 15 of 18 newly infected health zones across five consecutive weeks of forecasts, 10.3 percentage points above the best existing Bayesian model (about 73%).

A finding that runs through all the experiments is the synergy that emerges when statistical covariates and foundation-model embeddings are used together. Statistical covariates provide interpretable, explicit signals, while PDFM and AlphaEarth embeddings capture nonlinear patterns learned through large-scale pretraining. Google frames PPE as early-stage research, but says it lowers the barrier for researchers and humanitarian organizations to build models without a dedicated engineering team.

blocks.cap: QuEra's neutral-atom quantum computer

blocks.x: QuEra Computing said it restored a quantum computer's laser system in seconds using software written by an AI agent. The company says this could ease the burden of needing an expert at every machine installed at a customer site.

The Boston-based company said in a press release that Anthropic's Claude wrote and tested the control program itself. The laser system, subjected to hundreds of disturbances in simulation and in the real environment, was recovered using that program. The work was done in a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a framework built for AI agents to operate lab and production equipment within defined safety limits.

QuEra's computer manipulates neutral atoms using precisely controlled lasers, and these atoms serve as qubits. Even a small frequency drift halts computation and requires re-establishing what is called the laser lock. Common failures are already auto-recovered, and the 256-qubit Aquila, available on Amazon Braket, maintains over 99% uptime. What remained were the complex failures that required human judgment.

Previously, four experts spent two to three weeks hand-writing recovery scripts. Even then, those scripts could only handle failures that engineers had anticipated and coded for in advance. The company handed this problem to Claude through MHS. The agent experimented on a dedicated laser testbed, evaluated the results, and revised its approach, running nonstop overnight through hundreds of failure cases.

Engineers set the limits on the agent's operation and reviewed its output. People also set the success criteria. On the hardware side, engineers specified safety boundaries, interlocks, and emergency-stop procedures for the agent to follow. Once development finished, Claude let go of the laser. What remains is an ordinary program that engineers can inspect and verify, and recovery is now handled by that program without any AI model's judgment.

Across 700 trials spanning seven failure types, the controller returned the laser to its target state 695 times. It never falsely reported success after a failed recovery. The company said the five failures stemmed from issues with the experimental apparatus, not controller defects. Most recoveries finished within 6 seconds, and even the hardest cases took 10 to 14 seconds, a task that typically takes a person 5 to 10 minutes.

The testbed sat not in an isolated test chamber but inside an active lab where people came and went, and every disturbance that arose naturally during the trial period was recovered without human hands. The configuration the agent found cut remaining noise to a fifth and also prevented the lock from slipping during unattended operation. Applying the same approach to lasers of other wavelengths, the system tuned its configuration through an unattended overnight run, a task that would otherwise take weeks.

“For years, the hardest part of scaling up quantum computers wasn't the physics, it was the person driving in at 2 a.m. to fix a laser lock,” said Sergio H. Cantu, QuEra's vice president of quantum systems. Still, this trial covered only a single subsystem, and it is not proof that an entire quantum computer can look after itself. MHS was launched jointly by Anthropic and the Janelia Research Campus of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, and it remains a limited research preview while its safety design is under review.

The personalized cancer vaccine developed jointly by Moderna and Merck would, if approved, become the first medicine whose genetic content is effectively written by an algorithm. For each patient, software scans thousands of tumor mutations and selects 34 neoantigens to include in that person's own mRNA vaccine.

blocks.cap: An mRNA strand replicated six times. Credit: Christine Kao/STAT

blocks.x: STAT's Meghana Keshavan points to how this experiment sits at the overlap of regulation and computation. Some researchers see the algorithm that picks the mutations as the treatment's 'secret sauce.' Skeptical investors on Wall Street, however, suspect the personalization itself may not even be necessary, arguing that the mRNA may simply be stimulating tumors to respond better to Keytruda.

So what is actually inside that algorithm? Alex Rubinsteyn, a cancer vaccine expert at the University of North Carolina, had a short answer. “No one really knows. Everyone claims what they have is proprietary knowledge.”

The money has already started moving. A week after announcing phase 3 success for its personalized cancer vaccine, Moderna is raising $2 billion through convertible notes. The same day's edition of The Readout also carried an analysis of how U.S. restrictions on Chinese biotech could benefit Europe, the shadow that AstraZeneca and Ionis's phase 3 failure of eplontersen casts over Alnylam, and news of the approval of Revolution Medicines's pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque.

The movement and sleep that wearables track only indirectly reflect glucose control. A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) uses a sensor under the skin to measure interstitial glucose every few minutes, directly recording fasting, overnight, and post-meal patterns. What remains is the problem of interpretation. Clinical labels that could read those trajectories are expensive and scarce.

GlucoFM, released on August 26 by a team led by Ahmed A. Metwally and Zechen Li at Google Research, answers this with self-supervised learning. While existing CGM foundation models such as CGMformer, GluFormer, and CGM-JEPA treat glucose as a single representational stream, GlucoFM encodes it as two separate branches: a slow baseline trend and the short-term deviations created by meals, activity, and sensor noise. It also does not discard time-of-day information or the location of missing values.

blocks.cap: GlucoFM overview. Data preprocessing, JEPA-style pretraining architecture, and clinical prediction applications. Credit: Google Research

blocks.x: Pretraining used 109,066 hours of unlabeled CGM data and 477 participant/session records gathered from Wear-CGM and four public datasets. Each record was fit to a 24-hour, 5-minute grid, with an observation mask kept to distinguish measured values from gaps. Rather than reconstructing raw values directly, the model was trained to infer the latent representation of masked segments from surrounding context, while also predicting how the baseline and short-term deviations would move over the next hour.

blocks.cap: GlucoFM's model architecture and pretraining objectives. Credit: Google Research
